title: The inner ruler
hook: the salt-and-banyan father of the Chandogya steps up as a challenger and hears of the one who lives inside everything, unseen
carry: the inner ruler lives in every being
tomorrow: Gargi stands up again with two questions like arrows. what are they?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gargi asked what everything is woven on, all the way to the top, until Yajnavalkya stopped her. Your line was everything is woven on Brahman.

An old friend steps up. In the Chandogya, Uddalaka Aruni was the father who dropped salt in water and split a banyan seed for his son, and said: you are that. Now he stands up in Janaka's court as a challenger, and like Bhujyu, he brings a question from a spirit. Years ago, he says, a spirit speaking through a woman asked us: do you know the thread that strings this world, the next world and all beings together? Do you know the inner controller? Yajnavalkya, if you drive off those cows without knowing them, your head will fall off.
screen: `THE FATHER FROM THE CHANDOGYA.` → `A SPIRIT'S QUESTION.` → `THE THREAD, AND THE CONTROLLER.`

segments.voice: I know them, Yajnavalkya says. Anyone can say I know, I know, says Uddalaka. Tell us. The thread, says Yajnavalkya, is wind: like a string through beads, it holds this world and the next together. Then the inner controller, in a long chant. He who lives in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules the earth from within: he is your self, the inner controller, the deathless. Then the same lines for water, fire, the sun, all beings. Then it turns inward: the breath, the eye, the mind. And the close. He is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower. There is no other seer but him. And Uddalaka falls silent. This is the antaryamin, the inner ruler, one of the great Hindu pictures of the divine: not only above the world, but inside every part of it, nearer than the thing itself knows. Ramanuja, the Vishishtadvaita teacher, took the phrase whose body the earth is and taught that the world and every soul are the body of God, who lives within them. Shankara, the Advaita teacher, read the inner controller as the one self. Either way, the person in front of you has someone living in them they may never have noticed. It's one way many Hindus explain namaste: folded hands for the one who lives inside the other.
screen: `ANYONE CAN SAY I KNOW, I KNOW.` · `THE THREAD IS WIND.` · `WHOSE BODY THE EARTH IS.` · `THE UNSEEN SEER.` · then, large: `THE INNER RULER LIVES IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: Feel the breath, and let the line come: lives in the breath, yet other than the breath. Then the resting eyes, then the mind with all its traffic: lives in it, yet the mind doesn't know it. If you pray, fold your hands for a moment at the end; if not, just rest them. Notice whether something steady seems to sit under each of these, watching.
Uddalaka. The teacher who asked about the thread and the antaryamin, the inner controller: the one who lives in each thing, whom the thing doesn't know, and who rules it from within.
Your line: the inner ruler lives in every being. Tomorrow, Gargi comes back, with two questions like two arrows. Until then.

howItsDone: The antaryamin passage is central in Sri Vaishnava theology, where God is understood as the inner ruler of all; students of other Vedanta schools study it too, and many Hindus explain the folded hands of namaste as honoring the divine within the other person.

fork.setup: the inner controller lives in the earth, and the earth does not know him. what does that mean for a stranger you pass on the street?
options: the same inner ruler lives in them, unseen, whether they know it or not.
nothing; only holy people have an inner ruler.
only people who know about him have him inside.
fork.reveal: he lives in all beings, and they don't know him. knowing isn't the condition; he's there either way.

original.note: Sanskrit antaryāmin: antar (within) + yam (to hold, to rule): the one who rules from within.

trapdoor: what you thought: a controller, like someone pulling strings.
what it means: the one who lives in each thing, other than it, unknown by it, its inmost self.
what a scholar hears: the antaryāmi brāhmaṇa (3.7) is a key text for Ramanuja's śarīra-śarīri teaching, the world as God's body; Shankara reads it as the one self.

Uddalaka Aruni.meaning: the Chandogya's teacher of salt and seed, now a challenger

antaryamin.meaning: the inner controller, who rules each thing from within

Ramanuja.meaning: a teacher of Vishishtadvaita: the world as God's body

Vishishtadvaita.meaning: the Vedanta school of one God with souls and world as his body

Shankara.meaning: a great teacher of Advaita Vedanta

namaste.meaning: a greeting with folded hands; literally, a bow to you

recall: the small space in the heart
